title: PAUL HEALED THE SICK—SO WHY DID HE LEAVE TROPHIMUS BEHIND SICK?
paragraphs:
PAUL HEALED THE SICK—SO WHY DID HE LEAVE TROPHIMUS BEHIND SICK?
One forgotten sentence near the end of Paul’s life destroys a dangerous illusion about faith, healing, suffering, and what it really means to trust Jesus when the miracle you prayed for does not come.
There is a sentence in the Bible that some Christians probably wish were not there.
It is only a few words.
Easy to read.
Easier to skip.
But if you have ever prayed until your voice trembled...
If you have ever believed God for healing and watched the sickness remain...
If you have ever asked why someone faithful to Jesus still suffered...
If you have ever wondered whether an unanswered prayer meant your faith was too small...
You need to sit with this verse.
Because the man writing it was Paul.
Yes.
That Paul.
The apostle through whom God performed extraordinary miracles.
The man whose ministry in Ephesus was accompanied by such remarkable works of God that Acts 19:11–12 describes the sick being healed in connection with handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched him.
Paul had watched God heal.
Paul had watched demons flee.
Paul had seen the supernatural power of Christ displayed in ways most of us have never witnessed.
And yet, near the end of his life, Paul quietly wrote something astonishing:
“Erastus abode at Corinth: but Trophimus have I left at Miletum sick.”
—2 Timothy 4:20, KJV
Read the last part again.
“Trophimus have I left at Miletum sick.”
Not healed.
Not instantly restored.
Not traveling triumphantly beside Paul with a testimony about his miracle.
Sick.
The Greek is even more striking:
“Τρόφιμον δὲ ἀπέλιπον ἐν Μιλήτῳ ἀσθενοῦντα.”
Trophimon de apelipon en Milētō asthenounta.
In straightforward English:
“But Trophimus I left in Miletus, being sick.”
The word ἀσθενοῦντα, asthenounta, comes from ἀσθενέω and speaks of being weak, ill, or sick.
There is no complicated theological escape hatch hidden inside the Greek.
Trophimus was sick.
Paul left him there.
And suddenly a question walks into the room that shallow Christianity does not always know how to answer:
Why?
Why didn't Paul simply heal him?
Why didn't he lay hands on him?
Why didn't he command the illness to leave?
Why didn't Paul tell Trophimus that if he possessed enough faith he would immediately recover?
Scripture does not tell us.
And that matters.
We must never pretend God revealed an explanation that He did not reveal.

We do not know the medical nature of Trophimus's illness. We are not told exactly how long it lasted. We are not told whether Paul prayed for his healing. We are not told whether Trophimus was eventually healed.
And we certainly are not told that Trophimus remained sick because he lacked faith.
That conclusion is not in the text.
What Scripture gives us is simultaneously simpler and more unsettling:
A faithful servant of Christ was sick.
An apostle with a genuine ministry of miracles knew about it.
And the sick believer was still left behind sick.
Trophimus was not some rebellious stranger wandering around the edges of Christianity.
Acts 20:4 places him among Paul's traveling companions.
Acts 21:29 identifies him as “Trophimus an Ephesian.”
He had traveled with Paul.
He had served.
He had been there.

In fact, Trophimus became unintentionally connected with one of the most explosive episodes of Paul's life. When Paul was in Jerusalem, some Jews from Asia saw Trophimus with him in the city and assumed Paul had taken this Gentile into the temple. That accusation helped ignite the uproar surrounding Paul's arrest.
Trophimus knew what costly association with Paul looked like.
He was not merely a spectator.
He was part of the story.
And still...
he got sick.
That sentence should shatter one of the cruelest lies sometimes whispered into suffering Christians:
“If you were really walking closely with God, this wouldn't be happening.”
Tell that to Trophimus.
Tell that to Timothy, whom Paul advised concerning his “frequent infirmities” in 1 Timothy 5:23.
Tell that to Epaphroditus, who, according to Philippians 2:27, became so sick that he nearly died.
And then look at Paul himself.

In 2 Corinthians 12, Paul describes a “thorn in the flesh.” Christians disagree about precisely what that thorn was, and Scripture does not identify it as a particular disease. We should therefore resist confidently diagnosing Paul from twenty centuries away.
But we do know something much more important.
Paul pleaded with the Lord three times for it to depart.
And God's answer was not the removal Paul requested.
It was grace.
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.”
—2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV
Do you see what Scripture is doing?
It is dismantling the idea that God's faithfulness can be measured only by whether suffering immediately disappears.
Sometimes God delivers you from the furnace.
Sometimes God meets you inside it.
Sometimes chains fall off.
Sometimes, like Paul near the end of 2 Timothy, you are still in confinement.
Sometimes Peter walks out of prison after an angel opens the doors.
And sometimes James is killed by the sword.
Same Christ.
Same Gospel.
Same sovereign God.
Different providences.
That does not mean we stop praying for healing.
Absolutely not.
James 5:14–16 explicitly calls believers to pray for the sick.
Jesus taught His disciples to ask.
The early church prayed.
Paul prayed.
We should pray boldly because God really does heal.
We should pray expectantly because nothing is impossible for Him.
We should pray persistently because Christ invites His people to bring their needs before God.
But biblical faith does not say, “God must answer exactly the way I demand or His promises are false.”
Biblical faith says, “My Father can deliver me. I will ask Him to deliver me. But even when I cannot understand His providence, I will not abandon Him.”
There is a world of difference.
And maybe that is where this verse finds you.
Maybe your name is not Trophimus.
But you know Miletus.
Your Miletus might be a hospital room.
A doctor's report.
An empty chair.
A prayer request you have repeated so many times that you no longer know what words to use.
Maybe everybody celebrated someone else's miracle while you quietly went home carrying the same pain.
Maybe you watched testimonies online.
“God healed me.”
“God restored me.”
“God answered overnight.”
And you were happy for them.
You really were.
But somewhere underneath the smile was a question you were ashamed to say aloud:
Jesus...
what about me?
That question can become unbearable when Christians give simplistic answers God Himself never gave.
“Maybe you didn't believe enough.”
“Maybe you didn't declare it correctly.”
“Maybe you spoke negatively.”
“Maybe you need to sow something.”
No.
Be careful before placing a burden on wounded people that Scripture itself does not place on Trophimus.
The Bible does not say:
“Trophimus I left sick in Miletus because he lacked faith.”
It says:
“Trophimus I left at Miletum sick.”
Period.
Sometimes the most faithful thing theology can say is, “God has not told us why.”
That is not unbelief.
That is humility.
We know God can heal.
We know God does heal.
We know Christians should pray for healing.
And we also know from Scripture itself that faithful Christians experienced sickness that was not immediately removed.
Those truths can exist in the same Bible because the center of Christianity was never perfect health in this present age.
The center is Jesus Christ.
This is where everything changes.
Because Christianity does not ultimately promise that if you follow Jesus closely enough, nothing painful will happen to you.
Christianity announces something infinitely greater:
The Son of God entered our suffering.
Jesus Christ took flesh.
He experienced hunger.
Weariness.
Rejection.
Grief.
Betrayal.
Pain.
And eventually a Roman cross.
At Calvary, the sinless Christ was crucified for sinners.
Not because suffering defeated Him.
Not because the Father lost control.
Christ willingly laid down His life.
The scandal of the cross looked like defeat.
Then Sunday came.
The stone was rolled away.
The crucified Christ rose bodily from the grave.
Death did not get the final sentence.
Jesus did.
And this is why Christian hope is greater than temporary relief.
Even every physical healing in this present world is temporary.
Lazarus was raised, but Lazarus eventually faced mortality again.
Everyone Jesus healed during His earthly ministry eventually died.
The Gospel promises something greater than merely postponing death.
It promises resurrection.
Revelation 21 points toward the day when God will wipe away every tear and death will be no more.
That is where Christian healing ultimately ends.
Not merely with a better medical report.
With resurrection.
With Christ.
With bodies raised imperishable.
With death swallowed up in victory.
So when Trophimus lies sick in Miletus, Christianity has not failed.
When Paul carries weakness, Christianity has not failed.
When Epaphroditus nearly dies, Christianity has not failed.
And when your prayer has not yet received the answer you desperately wanted, Jesus has not suddenly stopped being Lord.
Your unanswered question is not proof of His absence.
Your hospital bed is not proof of His rejection.
Your weakness is not automatically evidence that God is disappointed with you.
And your suffering does not erase the cross.
Maybe you needed those words tonight.
Because perhaps you have secretly been angry with God.
Perhaps you have been performing Christianity while something inside you has been screaming:
“Why didn't You stop it?”
“Why didn't You heal them?”
“Why didn't You answer me?”
“Why did You let me walk through this?”
God is not threatened by the fact that you hurt.
Bring the grief to Him.
Bring the confusion.
Bring the questions.
Bring the disappointment.
But bring them to Jesus.
Do not run from the only One who can ultimately redeem what suffering has broken.
And there is another side to Trophimus's story that should confront us.
Imagine being left behind.
Paul continues.
The mission continues.
Other people keep moving.
But you cannot.
Have you ever watched life continue without you?
People are building careers while you are surviving.
People are celebrating marriages while yours is collapsing.
People are posting family pictures while you are grieving someone nobody can replace.
People are preaching victory while you can barely get out of bed.
People seem to be moving forward...
and you feel left in Miletus.
Listen carefully.
Being left in Miletus did not mean Trophimus had been left by Christ.
Those are not the same thing.
Your usefulness to God is not measured by your ability to keep pace with everybody else.
You are not loved because you can perform.
You are loved in Christ because grace is grace.
There are seasons when faith looks like running.
There are seasons when faith looks like standing.
And there are seasons when faith looks like lying in weakness and whispering:
“Jesus, I still trust You.”
Maybe nobody applauds that kind of faith.
Heaven sees it.
There is something profoundly beautiful about a believer who worships God after the outcome becomes uncertain.
Anyone can praise when the answer arrives exactly as requested.
But there is a different depth in the trembling voice that says:
“I still believe You are good.”
Not because the pain feels good.
Not because sickness is good.
Not because evil should be renamed blessing.
But because the character of God is not rewritten by the worst chapter of our lives.
And perhaps that is the deeper battle behind your suffering.
The enemy would love to use your pain to rewrite your theology of God.
“He abandoned you.”
“He forgot you.”
“You are being punished.”
“Prayer doesn't matter.”
“Jesus doesn't care.”
But then the cross stands in the middle of history and answers:
Look again.
The God Christians worship is not watching human agony from a safe distance.
In Christ, He stepped into our world.
Jesus wept.
Jesus bled.
Jesus suffered.
Jesus died.
And Jesus rose.
The cross means your sin can be forgiven.
The resurrection means your suffering does not own the ending.
Maybe your greatest need right now is not an explanation.
Maybe it is reconciliation.
Because sickness is terrible, but Scripture identifies a deeper human catastrophe: sin separates us from the holy God who made us.
You can have a healthy body and still possess a dying soul.
You can receive the medical answer you wanted and still remain alienated from God.
That is why Jesus came for something deeper than making our present lives comfortable.
He came to save sinners.
He carried our sins to the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And the call of the Gospel is not “pretend everything is okay.”
It is:
Repent.
Believe.
Come to Christ.
Stop hiding.
Stop bargaining.
Stop trying to become clean enough before approaching Him.
Come as the sinner who needs mercy.
Come as the exhausted believer who needs grace.
Come as the wounded person who has questions.
Come to Jesus.
Maybe the scandal in your life is the thing you thought disqualified you.
The addiction nobody knows about.
The marriage you damaged.
The years you wasted.
The secret compromise.
The bitterness.
The pornography.
The pride.
The lies.
The night you wish you could erase.
The prayer that seems unanswered.
The diagnosis that changed everything.
The season when you became angry at God.
But this is the heartbeat of the Gospel:
Jesus Christ specializes in taking stories that look finished and writing grace where sin expected a period.
Peter denied Him.
Grace found Peter.
Paul persecuted His church.
Grace transformed Paul into a preacher of the Christ he once opposed.
The thief beside Jesus had almost no life left to repair.
Grace reached him at a cross.
That is why our heartbeat remains:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by promising every consequence disappears immediately.
He rewrites us through repentance, forgiveness, redemption, and a new life centered on Himself.
And maybe this article did not find you accidentally.
Maybe you have been quietly exhausted.
Maybe your faith has become performance.
Maybe you have been smiling publicly and bleeding privately.
Be honest.
Someone reading beneath you may desperately need to know that another believer has walked through darkness without letting go of Jesus.
Not because every sentence is easy.
Or someone you love will.
And when that day comes, you may need to remember:
Sickness does not mean Jesus abandoned you.
Not as a religious performance. Not as a way of purchasing God's favor. Christ alone saves.
Send it to the believer who feels ashamed because their prayer remains unanswered.
Sometimes sharing biblical truth is one small way we participate in making Christ known.
Do it as support for ministry, never as payment for God's blessing.
It cannot purchase healing.
It cannot earn salvation.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Come to Jesus.
Because eventually every one of us reaches a place where money cannot rescue us.
Medicine cannot make us immortal.
Influence cannot save us.
Religious performance cannot erase our sin.
And our own strength cannot carry us across death.
We need Christ.
Trophimus was left sick in Miletus.
Paul eventually approached the end of his earthly race.
The great apostle who had watched extraordinary miracles knew that his own departure was near.
Yet he could still say:
“I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith.”
That is victory.
Not that nothing ever hurt.
Not that every prayer was answered according to his preferred timetable.
Not that everybody around him was always healed.
Paul's victory was that Christ remained worthy all the way to the finish line.
So if you are standing beside someone else's hospital bed tonight...
If you are carrying a diagnosis...
If your body hurts...
If grief has rearranged your world...
If you are begging God for a miracle...
Ask.
Pray.
Believe that God is able.
Seek appropriate care.
Let the church surround you.
And never confuse unanswered questions with an absent Savior.
You may not know why this chapter was permitted.
Trophimus's single sentence reminds us that Scripture does not always give us the why.
But the Gospel tells us who holds the ending.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
Reigning.
Coming again.
And when He finally makes all things new, no child of God will look back at resurrection glory and conclude that death won.
So until then...
pray for the miracle.
And trust Jesus when you cannot explain the waiting.
Ask for healing.
And cling to Christ when healing has not yet come.
Cry when it hurts.
And refuse to let suffering convince you that Calvary was a lie.
Because sometimes the strongest faith in the room is not the person shouting that a miracle is coming.
Sometimes it is the wounded believer whispering through tears:
“Even here, Jesus... I am still Yours.”
There is no prize for pretending you are strong when your heart is exhausted.
Your Miletus may explain why you are crying tonight—but it does not get to write the final chapter of a story that belongs to Jesus.
